newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: G10 central bankers say inflation remains in check.
newsitem.headline: G10 central bankers say inflation remains in check.

text.p: Group of 10 (G10) central bankers see inflation still moderate in Europe despite a firm dollar, and in spite of signs of improved growth in some countries, Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer said on Monday.

The dollar's recent gains were starting to put some upward pressure on European prices, Tietmeyer said, briefing journalists after a meeting of G10 central bankers at the Bank for International Settlements here.

Tietmeyer is chairman of the G10 central bank governors committee. The G10, which in fact is 11 countries, comprises the U.S., Japan, Germany, Canada, Belgium, the Netherlands, Britain, France, Italy, Sweden and Switzerland.
"All in all, inflation is still under control," Tietmeyer told reporters.
G10 governors also discussed foreign exchange markets at their monthly meeting, but Tietmeyer said the market seemed "relatively quiet".
"In Europe we see some effects on the import price side of the strength of the dollar in the last months," Tietmeyer said.
The dollar has risen steadily in recent months, trading at roughly 1.7060 marks in Europe on Monday afternoon. That compared with levels closer to 1.46 marks late last July.
Tietmeyer said that the impact on import prices varies from country to country, depending on the openness of the economies with respect to international trade.
"All in all, it is not the case that there is a new inflationary environment in Europe," he said, adding: "Monetary policy is more or less on the right track."
At the same time, the outlook for growth in G10 countries remains positive.

Tietmeyer said G10 central bank governors believed that economic growth was continuing in North America and the United Kingdom, and also said that growth in Japan appeared to be on a self-sustaining path.
In continental Europe, Tietmeyer said there was some improvement but the situation varied from country to country.

Addressing another matter of recent concern to financial markets, Tietmeyer said he had heard of no central banks planning further gold sales since Switzerland announced last week that it planned to put some reserve gold on the market in years ahead, providing legal changes are carried out.
Tietmeyer said the issue of central bank gold reserves was not discussed among G10 central bank governors on Monday at the BIS meeting.
"I haven't heard anybody who has indicated that he will do gold sales," Tietmeyer said.

Gold markets were unsettled by news last week that the Swiss National Bank, according to a proposal by the Swiss government, would revalue its gold reserves and give seven billion Swiss francs in reserve gold to a proposed humanitarian fund. The fund would sell the gold gradually over a period of up to 10 years.
The Swiss government's proposal must still be approved by parliament and by voters in a referendum sometime in 1998.
